2	title: Glossary
3	description: Frame Job's own words in plain terms, from action and canvas to nest, ramp, stem and tick, each linked to its page.
4	---
5	
6	The words Frame Job uses, in plain terms, each with a link to the page that explains it.
7	
8	## Projects and the timeline
9	
10	- **Action.** An animation on a clip: a span on its action lane with an end state its properties ease to. See [Actions](/motion/actions/).
11	- **Adjustment clip.** A clip with no picture of its own that grades every track behind it. See [Adjustment clips](/color/adjustment-clips/).
12	- **Canvas.** The fixed frame every clip is composited into. Every export starts from its size. See [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/).
13	- **Clip.** One placed piece on a track: a stretch of a media file, or a text, shape, image, graphic, adjustment or nest clip. See [Core concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/).
14	- **Current track.** The track of the first selected clip, or with nothing selected the front-most track. Track commands act on it. See [Menus](/reference/menus/).
15	- **Edit point.** A clip's start or end, where <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> stop. See [Jump around the timeline](/timeline/move-the-playhead/).
16	- **Frame grid.** The frames of the project's rate. Every time you set lands on one. See [Core concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/).
17	- **Identity.** An edit that was understood and had nothing to change. It beeps, makes no undo step and shows no message. See [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/).
18	- **In–Out range.** The span set with <kbd>I</kbd> and <kbd>O</kbd>, which many commands act on. See [The in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/).
19	- **Linked pair.** A picture clip and its detached sound, which move, split and ripple together. See [Detach and Attach Audio](/audio/detach-and-attach/).
20	- **Media.** A file the project has imported, listed in the Media tab. Clips refer to it. See [The Media tab](/projects/media-tab/).
21	- **Nest.** A clip that wraps other clips into a timeline of its own. See [Nests](/editing/nests/).
22	- **Package.** A `.framejob` project, a folder the Finder shows as one file. See [The .framejob package](/reference/framejob-package/).
23	- **Playhead.** The current time on the timeline. See [The ruler and playhead](/timeline/ruler-and-playhead/).
24	- **Refusal.** A rule declining an edit, in that rule's own sentence. Nothing changes and no undo step is made. See [When an edit is refused](/getting-started/refused-edits/).
25	- **Ripple.** An edit that closes the gap it leaves by moving later clips along. See [Delete, Ripple Delete and Lift](/editing/delete-clips/).
26	- **Selected action.** The one action of the single selected clip that the Clip tab is editing. While it's chosen, the fields show and write its end state. See [Select an action](/motion/select-an-action/).
27	- **Tick.** Frame Job's unit of time, 600,000 to the second, which divides every common frame duration exactly. Refusals and agents speak in ticks. See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).
28	- **Track.** A lane of clips. The front track is the top lane, and it's drawn over those behind it. See [Tracks](/timeline/tracks/).
29	
30	## Picture and sound
31	
32	- **Camera Log.** A file's setting saying which camera log curve it holds, so it's converted at the start of the picture. See [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/).
33	- **Cue.** One timed caption. See [Captions are text clips](/captions/how-captions-work/).
34	- **Cutout.** A clip with Remove Background on. See [Remove Background](/effects/remove-background/).
35	- **Deep.** More than 8 bits a component. See [Precision and bit depth](/hdr/precision/).
36	- **Ducking.** Lowering a clip's sound under another's. See [Ducking](/audio/ducking/).
37	- **Dynamic range.** Whether the project works in SDR or HDR (HLG). See [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/).
38	- **J-cut and L-cut.** The sound of a linked pair starting before, or ending after, its picture. See [J-cuts and L-cuts](/audio/j-and-l-cuts/).
39	- **Look.** A built-in grade or a `.cube` LUT on a clip. See [Looks](/color/looks/).
40	- **LUFS.** The unit of loudness. See [Normalize](/audio/normalize/).
41	- **LUT.** A colour lookup table in a `.cube` file. See [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/).
42	- **Matte.** A track that cuts the track behind it by its alpha or brightness. See [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/).
43	- **Plate.** A clip that fills the canvas behind everything, such as a solid colour or a picture from **Add Background**. See [Backgrounds](/canvas/backgrounds/).
44	- **Qualifier.** An adjustment clip's pick of the pixels it grades, by hue, saturation and brightness. See [Qualifiers](/color/qualifiers/).
45	- **Ramp.** A speed change over time, a Speed action on the action lane. See [Speed ramps](/speed/speed-ramps/).
46	- **Scopes.** The waveform, parade, vectorscope and histogram beside the preview. See [Scopes](/color/scopes/).
47	- **Slate.** What a clip draws in place of a picture it doesn't have, such as missing media. See [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/).
48	- **Stem.** One track's sound written as its own file beside the mix. See [Audio stems](/export/stems/).
49	- **Transition.** The change from one clip to the next across their overlap on one track. See [Transitions](/motion/transitions/).
50	
51	## Graphics and agents
52	
53	- **Assistant.** The chat in the inspector that edits the open project on your own Anthropic key. See [Chat with the Assistant](/assistant/chat/).
54	- **Category.** The list a module is filed under in the Graphic dialog. See [Bundled templates](/graphics/templates/).
55	- **Error card.** What a graphic draws in its own box when it can't draw itself. See [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/).
56	- **Graphic.** A clip whose picture is drawn by code. It's the clip's content, not an effect. See [What a graphic is](/graphics/what-is-a-graphic/).
57	- **Graphic package.** A `.fjgraphic` file holding a module and the fonts and pictures it uses. See [Share a graphic](/graphics/share-a-graphic/).
58	- **Kept revision.** An earlier text of a module the app kept, the last 10 for each module. See [Rename, delete and restore graphics](/graphics/manage-graphics/).
59	- **MCP.** The protocol an agent uses to drive Frame Job, through the `framejob-mcp` helper. See [How an agent reaches Frame Job](/mcp/overview/).
60	- **Module.** A graphic's source, one JavaScript module returning SVG for each frame. See [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/).
61	- **Op.** One edit to a project, applied whole. An agent's tools mostly each send one. See [How tool calls behave](/mcp/tool-calls/).
62	- **Patch.** A partial object a caller writes to say what to change. See [Patches](/mcp/patches/).
63	- **Props.** The values a graphic is drawn with, stored on its clip. See [Graphic properties](/graphics/properties/).
64	- **Template.** A module the app ships, copied into the package when you insert it. See [Bundled templates](/graphics/templates/).

15	## Frame Job's licence
16	
17	Frame Job is released under the Apache License, Version 2.0. The full text is the [LICENSE file](https://github.com/kpgalligan/framejob/blob/main/LICENSE) at the root of the repository.
18	
19	## Third-party notices
20	
21	Every copy of the app carries `Acknowledgements.txt`, which lists every third-party notice the app owes, each with its licence text. It's written at each build, from the Rust crates, the Assistant helper's npm packages, Bun, Sparkle, the encoders, the voice-activity model and the fonts.
22	
23	There's no entry for it in the About panel. To read it:
24	
25	<Steps>

27	1. In the Finder, right-click Frame Job and choose **Show Package Contents**.
28	
29	2. Open `Contents/Resources/Acknowledgements.txt`.
30	
31	</Steps>

35	Some of what ships with Frame Job keeps its own licence, beside it in the app or listed in `Acknowledgements.txt`.
36	
37	| Part | Licence | Where its text is |

1	---
2	title: When an edit is refused
3	description: How Frame Job tells you it won't make an edit, from the Refused strip in the inspector to a beep with no message, and why nothing changes.
4	---
5	
6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
7	
8	Frame Job has rules that keep a project sound, such as how far two clips may overlap. When an edit would break one, nothing changes and Frame Job says so. How it says so tells you what happened.
9	
10	<AtAGlance
11	  where={['The foot of the inspector', 'The timeline, for a drop']}
12	/>
13	
14	| What you see | What happened |
15	| --- | --- |
16	| A beep and a **Refused:** line at the foot of the inspector | A rule wouldn't allow the edit |
17	| A clip animates back to the last place it was allowed | The rules wouldn't allow the drop |
18	| A beep and no message | The edit would have changed nothing |
19	| An error alert | Frame Job couldn't use the request at all |
20	
21	Only a drop can still move the clip, to the last allowed place on its way. None of the others changes the project or makes an undo step.
22	
23	## The refusal strip
24	
25	When a rule won't allow an edit, Frame Job beeps and shows the rule's own sentence at the foot of the inspector, after "Refused: ":
26	
27	> Refused: track 3 is locked, so the gap on it cannot be closed
28	
29	The strip shows up to three lines. Rest the pointer on it to read the whole sentence.
30	
31	It stays until you click it or the project changes, which means an edit, an undo or redo, or going into or out of a nest. Moving the playhead or changing the selection doesn't clear it, so you can look around while you work out what to do.
32	
33	The sentence is exact rather than friendly. It can name clips and tracks by Frame Job's own numbers, which aren't their positions on the timeline, and give lengths in the timeline's smallest units rather than in seconds.
34	
35	Each feature's page lists what can stop it, and [Troubleshooting](/reference/troubleshooting/) gathers them in one place.
36	
37	A typed Start, Length or end value on an action shows the strip too. Dragging an action's band never does. See [Move, resize or remove an action](/motion/change-an-action/).
38	
39	## A drop that springs back
40	
41	While you drag, positions the rules don't allow are skipped and the clip waits at the last allowed one. A clip dropped on one of those positions animates back to that place and stays there, as one undo step. If the drag never reached an allowed place, it animates back to where it started and nothing changes. See [Move clips](/editing/move-clips/).
42	
43	## A beep with no message
44	
45	An edit that would change nothing beeps but shows no message, because no rule was broken. A slip does this when the clip is already at the end of its footage, and **Edit ▸ Paste Attributes** does it on clips that already have the copied look.
46	
47	## An error alert
48	
49	Now and then Frame Job can't use a request at all, such as a value outside its allowed range. It shows an error alert naming the offending value. You'll rarely meet one, because the inspector's number fields already [hold what you type to their range](/getting-started/inspector-fields/#type-a-value).
50	
51	## With an agent
52	
53	An agent is told the same things in words. An edit a rule won't allow fails with the rule's sentence, and an edit that changes nothing fails saying so. See [What a call answers](/mcp/what-a-call-answers/).
54	
55	## Related
56	
57	- [Undo and saving](/getting-started/undo-and-saving/)
58	- [Troubleshooting](/reference/troubleshooting/)
59	- [How edits work](/editing/how-edits-work/)
60

/// A rule declined the op, in the rule's own words. **No undo step**,
    /// exactly as for an identity — a refusal is not an error tier and the
    /// project is left exactly as it was — but the caller is told why.
    ///
    /// The sentence is the one the rule itself writes, passed through
    /// verbatim so it is written once: "clips 3 and 4 would overlap by 8000
    /// ticks, more than half of the shorter clip (6000 ticks)". It names
    /// what a caller could act on, and it is prose, not a code.
    ///
    /// **Every rule's sentence names the value, not the rule.** Which track
    /// is locked, which clips still show the media, how many frames the cut
    /// has left, which action is in the way: a caller that reads one knows
    /// what to send instead without asking the project again. Where an
    /// argument would let the op through, the sentence names that argument
    /// (`with_clips: true`, `ripple: true`) — advice a caller can act on,
    /// not a second description of the rule. A rule with more than one site
    /// writes its sentence once and the sites pass a clause
    /// (`edit_time::locked_track`, `edit_action`'s two, `edit_track`'s
    /// `clip_list`), so two ops cannot drift apart on the same rule.
    Refused(String),
}

## MCP

This section shows how an MCP client, such as Claude Code, reaches Frame Job. Clients use `framejob-mcp`, a helper inside the app, which connects over a local socket that only programs you run can open. If Frame Job isn't running, the first tool call opens it in the background.

Under that text is the full path of the helper inside the copy you're running. You can select and copy it.

**Copy MCP Command** puts the line that registers the helper with Claude Code on the clipboard, with the path filled in and quoted for the shell:

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user framejob -- '/Applications/Frame Job.app/Contents/Helpers/framejob-mcp'
```

The section then says "Copied. Paste it into Terminal and press Return."

The path is always the one for the app you opened Settings from, so copy the command again if you move Frame Job. If the helper is missing from this copy, the button is dimmed and the section says "framejob-mcp is missing from this copy of Frame Job."

The command is for Claude Code. Other clients use the same helper path in their own configuration. See [Connect a client](/mcp/connect-a-client/).

return "\(fileName) is AV1 video, which needs an M3 or later Mac."
        case kCMVideoCodecType_AV1:
            return "\(fileName) is AV1 video, which this Mac cannot decode."
        case kCMVideoCodecType_VP9:
            if let profile = vp9Profile, profile == 1 || profile == 3 {
                return "\(fileName) is VP9 Profile \(profile) video, which this Mac cannot decode;"
                    + " VP9 Profiles 0 and 2 import."
            }
            return "\(fileName) is VP9 video, which this Mac cannot decode."
        case vp8:
            return "\(fileName) is VP8 video, which this Mac cannot decode."
        case 0:
            return "\(fileName) is video this Mac cannot decode."
        default:
            let code = String([24, 16, 8, 0].map {
                Character(Unicode.Scalar(UInt8((codec >> UInt32($0)) & 0xFF)))
            })
            return "\(fileName) is '\(code)' video, which this Mac cannot decode."
        }
    }

    /// The sentence for a track with these descriptions: the first one's
    /// codec and VP9 profile, and whether this Mac decodes AV1 in hardware.
    static func refusal(fileName: String, descriptions: [CMFormatDescription]) -> String {
        let first = descriptions.first
        return refusal(
            fileName: fileName, codec: first.map { CMFormatDescriptionGetMediaSubType($0) } ?? 0,
            vp9Profile: first.flatMap { vp9Profile(of: $0) },
            av1Hardware: VTIsHardwareDecodeSupported(kCMVideoCodecType_AV1))
    }
}

18:## Hit a loudness target
32:## The Loudness popup
38:| **Off** | No normalisation. The export still goes through the master limiter, measures its sound and reports it. |
50:## How normalisation works
56:The gain is worked out through the master limiter, so the file lands on the target even when its loudest peaks would pass the ceiling. Those peaks are turned down, not the whole mix.
60:## The master limiter
62:Every export with sound goes through a true-peak limiter, normalised or not. True peak is the highest the sound really reaches, including between samples, and dBTP is its unit. The limiter keeps the file's true peak at or under **−1 dBTP**. A mix that would pass that is limited instead of clipped, whether the cause is loud clips, a crossfade between two loud clips, a nest turned up or an action that raises a clip's volume.
65:- The limiter holds the sound back 3.3 ms to see each peak coming, and releases over 100 ms. The export takes that delay back, so the sound stays exactly in sync with the picture.
69:The preview has no master limiter, so a mix that passes −1 dBTP sounds louder while you edit than it does in the file.
72:## Track compressors in the export
74:A track's own [compressor and limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/) run before the master, on that track's sound alone, exactly as you set them. The export plays each such track on its own through them and mixes the tracks afterwards.
78:The master is only the loudness gain and the limiter. There's no master compressor or EQ. To compress the whole mix, [nest](/editing/nests/) everything onto one track and give that track a compressor.
80:## What the loudness line means
89:| `… · peaks limited by 8.6 dB` | The master limiter turned the loudest peak down by that much to hold the ceiling. It appears from 0.05 dB. |
94:## Good to know
98:- The figures describe the mix. Stems aren't measured, and they get no target or master limiter.
100:## With an agent
104:An agent can also choose a different ceiling for the master limiter with `peak_dbtp`, which the sheet doesn't offer. It runs from −20 to 0 dBTP, is −1 when left out, and works with or without a target. 0 dBTP is the loosest, and there's no way to turn the limiter off.

112:- [Track compressor and limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/)
